differentiation.extension: Choose one claim your team lost the debate on. Prepare a one-minute rebuttal that connects that claim to the wider ten-year timeline (1789–1799): how might this cause have contributed to later events such as political radicalization or Napoleon’s rise? Cite at least one specific event or date from the Revolution that could follow from your causal link.
differentiation.support: Pair a student who struggles to start with a stronger partner. Give this sentence frame and a worked example to the struggling student: ‘Short-term cause: [food shortages]. Evidence: “line 3: rising bread prices”’. Worked first item for them to copy: Short-term cause: rising bread prices. Evidence: line 3: ‘bread prices rose sharply in 1788–89’. Use only one claim if time is short.

materials: One printed short evidence sheet per pair (teacher can cut a single A4 into slips; see suggested extract lines below)
Timer or stopwatch
Paper and pen for each student
One sheet of chart paper or whiteboard space for each team to record main claims
student_instructions: Preparation (4 minutes): Read your pair’s evidence slip carefully. On your team chart paper, write two claims your team will argue: one short-term cause and one long-term cause of the 1789 Revolution. For each claim, copy the exact phrase or line number from your slip that supports it.

Debate (6 minutes): When your team speaks, each speaker has about 45 seconds. Present your two claims in clear order: say ‘Short-term cause: [claim], evidence: [quote or slip line].’ Then ‘Long-term cause: [claim], evidence: [quote or slip line].’ When responding, point out where you disagree and offer alternative evidence from your slip. Do not shout; keep to time.
Wrap-up (2 minutes): Together, post your chart paper with the two claims and their evidence lines. Be ready to point to the evidence if the teacher asks one question.
success_criteria: Each team posts a chart paper that shows two labelled claims (one short-term, one long-term) each with a copied quote or slip line number.
During the debate, at least one speaker from each team cites the slip by quoting a phrase or stating a line number aloud.
At least one team mentions the Bastille and either states or corrects the misconception by citing evidence about prisoner numbers or the Bastille’s symbolic role.
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in pairs and then combine two pairs into small debate teams (teams of four: two students pro, two students con). Give each pair one evidence slip and a blank team chart paper space. Announce: “You have 12 minutes total: 4 minutes prepare, 6 minutes debate, 2 minutes wrap-up.” Start the timer.

2. During the 4-minute preparation: circulate and prompt teams to list short-term causes and long-term causes from their slips, and to decide which two claims their team will defend. Remind them to cite the evidence slip line numbers aloud during debate.

3. Run the 6-minute debate as two timed rounds: Round A (3 minutes) — Team 1 presents their two claims with evidence (each speaker 45 seconds). Round B (3 minutes) — Team 2 responds and presents counter-claims with evidence (each speaker 45 seconds). Use the timer and call time at 30 seconds and 10 seconds left for each speaker.

4. For the 2-minute wrap-up: ask each team to post their chart paper summary (two claims + evidence lines, one short-term and one long-term cause). While students post, note any charts that mention the Bastille and whether they specify the misconception about political prisoners.

5. After activity ends, give one-minute feedback to the whole class: point out competing interpretations you observed and correct the Bastille misconception by stating the historical evidence (that the Bastille held few if any political prisoners on 14 July 1789).
activities.title: Mini-debate: What sparked the French Revolution in 1789?

differentiation.extension: Choose one pair's sentence on the board and write a 2-minute oral rebuttal that presents an alternative interpretation using at least one other historical factor (for example, argue that 'bad harvests' were amplified by tax complexity or by political resistance to reform). Prepare a 30-second explanation of which interpretation better links cause to the Estates General or to the onset of the Reign of Terror, citing evidence.
differentiation.support: If you cannot start: use this sentence frame and the worked example. Frame: 'This slip shows [long-term/short-term/sequence/Reign of Terror] because "[short quote]", so it supports [named cause].' Worked example: if your slip says 'bad harvests and rising bread prices', write: 'This slip shows a long-term economic/social cause because "bad harvests and rising bread prices" indicates repeated food shortages, which supports the claim that economic hardship contributed to revolution.' Pair a student who needs help with a more confident reader.

materials: One printed evidence slip per pair (teacher prepares 6 slips from the textbook or supplied document: two about long-term causes, two about short-term triggers, one about Estates General events, one about the Reign of Terror statistics)
Stopwatch or visible timer
Whiteboard or chart paper and marker for each group (or a pair share one)
student_instructions: 1. With your partner, quietly read the evidence slip for 2 minutes. Underline the exact words that show a cause (long-term or short-term), an action at the Estates General, or a fact about the Reign of Terror.

2. For 5 minutes discuss with your partner and then write one clear sentence on the chart paper that: names the cause or sequence your slip supports, quotes the underlined words, and states whether this is a long-term factor, a short-term trigger, an action in 1789, or a Reign of Terror statistic. Example sentence frame: 'This slip shows [short-term/long-term/sequence/Reign of Terror] because “[quote from slip]”, which supports [named cause or event].'

3. Together create one short question that challenges another interpretation of your slip (for example: 'Could this economic complaint be short-term rather than long-term? Why or why not?'). Be ready to read your sentence and question aloud in the round-robin.
4. When pairs speak in the round-robin, listen and note one piece of evidence you might add to their claim. At the end, raise your hand to vote on the contested item the teacher chooses.
success_criteria: Each pair has a sentence on chart paper that quotes the slip and labels it as a long-term factor, short-term trigger, Estates General action, or Reign of Terror statistic.
Pairs can point to the exact words on their slip they used to justify their labelled cause or sequence during the teacher's circulation.
During the round-robin at least two different interpretations of a single slip are recorded on the board (teacher sees at least one disagreement noted).
teacher_instructions: 1. Organize students into pairs. Give each pair one evidence slip, a sheet of chart paper (or a blank area on the board), and a marker. Display a visible 12-minute timer and announce the task: analyze this piece of evidence, decide which cause(s) it supports (long-term social, economic, financial, political; or short-term trigger), and whether it helps explain how the Estates General led to the National Assembly or provides evidence about the Reign of Terror.

2. Say: 'In two minutes quietly read your slip and underline the exact words that support a cause or a sequence of events. Then you have five minutes to talk with your partner and write one sentence on the chart that cites the evidence and names the cause or event it supports. Finish by preparing one question to challenge a different interpretation.' Start the timer for 2 minutes of silent reading; give a 30-second warning.

3. Start the five-minute paired discussion. While pairs work, circulate and listen: when you hear a pair argue about whether a slip is long-term or short-term, ask them to point to the words that made them decide. If a pair cannot start after the silent reading, give them the support scaffold (see Support).

4. After five minutes of paired discussion, call a 3-minute round-robin: each pair reads their one-sentence claim plus their challenge question aloud (limit 30 seconds per pair). Track time and prompt pairs to stop at 30 seconds. Record any differing interpretations on the class board under two columns labeled 'Causes/Sequence' and 'Reign of Terror evidence'.

5. In the final 2 minutes, ask the whole class to vote (show of hands) on one contested interpretation recorded on the board (teacher selects one contested item). Conclude by reading aloud the Reign of Terror statistic from the slip and say: 'Notice the statistic is evidence; what it does not show by itself is whether all revolutionaries supported mass repression.'
activities.title: Weighing Causes and Sequence: Small-Group Evidence Discussion

differentiation.extension: Ask fast-finishing groups to produce a 2-minute follow-up scene in which the Assembly tries to respond to priest resistance—have them use evidence to propose one policy change (e.g., compensation for clergy, phased implementation). They must cite which excerpt supports their proposed policy and explain how it might alter the social consequence they listed.
differentiation.support: Pair a less confident student with a steady partner and give them a reduced role slip that includes the exact sentence to read aloud and a one-line prompt: “Explain how this sentence shows why your character supports or opposes the Assembly.” Alternatively, give the group a worked example chart showing one measure, one consequence, and two interpretations.

materials: One printed role slip per student (priest, revolutionary deputy, peasant, noble, urban worker)

Short primary-source excerpt printed for each group (one sentence on: Declaration of the Rights of Man; August Decrees abolishing feudalism; Civil Constitution of the Clergy; notice of confiscation of church land)
One large sheet of paper or chart paper per group
Markers
Stopwatch or timer
student_instructions: You are in a group of five. Each of you has a role: priest, revolutionary deputy, peasant, noble, or urban worker. Read your role slip and the four short excerpts together.
Preparation (2 minutes): Decide quickly what your character wants and choose one excerpt sentence that supports your view. Be ready to say that sentence aloud during the role play.

Role play (6 minutes): Act out a short scene in which your character reacts to three Assembly measures: confiscation of church property, abolition of tithes, and the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. When you speak, read or paraphrase the single sentence of evidence from the excerpts that supports your position, then respond to another character once.

Group summary (3 minutes): On the chart paper write (a) the three measures the Assembly took, (b) one social consequence your group found in the excerpts (for example: division among clergy and Catholics; peasants relieved of tithes; state control of religion), and (c) two different interpretations of those consequences (why some supported and some resisted the changes).
success_criteria: Each student reads or paraphrases one sentence from the provided excerpts while in role during the play.
Each group’s chart lists the three measures (confiscation of church property, abolition of tithes/August Decrees, Civil Constitution of the Clergy) and records one social consequence.
At least two groups present two competing interpretations on their chart (one supportive view and one critical view) before the debrief ends.
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in groups of five. Give each student a role slip and give each group the four short primary-source excerpts (one sentence each). Say: “You will stage a 6-minute role play and a 3-minute group summary. Use the excerpts as your evidence.” Start the timer for 2 minutes of role preparation.

2. While groups prepare, circulate and check that each student can point to at least one sentence on their slip that supports their character's position (e.g., priest notes Civil Constitution line; deputy notes Declaration line). If a group lacks a clear evidence sentence, hand them one highlighted excerpt.

3. After 2 minutes, signal the 6-minute role play. Groups perform a short scene where characters argue over the Assembly’s measures: confiscation of church property, abolition of tithes, and the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Prompt with: “Show what each character wants, cite one sentence of evidence, and react to one other character.” Walk around and time-check at 3 minutes and 1 minute left.

4. After the role play, give groups 3 minutes to write a one-paragraph group summary on chart paper that (a) lists the three measures, (b) gives one social consequence mentioned in the sources, and (c) presents two competing interpretations (for example: reformers saw equality and financial necessity; some Catholics saw attack on religion and community). Collect or post the charts and end with a 1-minute whole-class debrief asking two groups to read their summaries.
activities.title: Debate at the National Assembly: Church Reforms Role Play

differentiation.extension: Choose two slips that appear to conflict (for example, a defender of the Law of 22 Prairial and a witness to drownings). On the back of your worksheet write a 3–4 sentence paragraph evaluating which account you find more credible and why, grounding your judgment in the text of the slips and noting what additional evidence you would need to decide between them (e.g., archival lists, trial records, other eyewitness accounts).
differentiation.support: Pair less-ready students with a stronger partner. Give the struggling pair this sentence starter for every station: 'This slip says __________ (fact). It shows disagreement because __________ (choose: different accounts, contested numbers, or a conflicting view).' Also provide a worked example on the first station: Slip text — 'Many bodies were drowned at Nantes; some contemporaries say hundreds, others say thousands.' Worksheet example — Fact: 'Contemporaries report drownings at Nantes; numbers vary.' Interpretation sentence: 'This shows disagreement because the slip gives two different death estimates.'

materials: 6 printed source slips (short quotations or claims) pinned or taped around the room — teacher prepares in 10 minutes
timer or stopwatch
one worksheet per student (one page) with space for observations and one evidence column
pens or pencils
clipboard or hard surface (optional)
student_instructions: Work with your partner. Take one worksheet and a pen. You will visit six stations. You have 1 minute at each station.

At each station: 1) Read the short slip silently together. 2) On your worksheet write a one-line factual note that is directly grounded in the slip (who, what, when). 3) Then write one sentence that answers: Does this slip suggest revolutionaries agreed on mass repression, or does it show disagreement? Give the line of evidence from the slip (quote or paraphrase).
When the teacher signals, rotate to the next station. Be punctual — you must move immediately when the signal is given.
After visiting all stations, return to your seat. Be ready to share one slip that showed disagreement and one slip about a disputed death estimate.
success_criteria: At each station a pair has written a factual note that accurately matches the wording of the slip (teacher can read worksheet and match to slip).
At least four pairs label at least three slips as showing disagreement among revolutionaries rather than unanimous support.
At least half the pairs copy or paraphrase an explicit number or phrase about deaths at Nantes or a phrase from the Law of 22 Prairial on their worksheet.
teacher_instructions: Before class (10 minutes): Prepare six short source slips (about 2–4 sentences each). Each slip presents a claim or piece of evidence directly tied to the concepts: (1) estimate of deaths at Nantes; (2) description of drownings at Nantes from a contemporary witness; (3) a short excerpt summarising the Law of 22 Prairial; (4) a Jacobin defender arguing the law sped trials for security; (5) an account of Robespierre's arrest, attempted suicide, injury, and execution on 28 July; (6) a historian's interpretation that Thermidor was a reaction against the Terror. Tape one slip at six stations around the room at about student eye level, and place a stack of worksheets at the front.

Step 1 (1 minute): Tell students: 'You will do a 12-minute gallery walk in pairs to gather evidence and note competing interpretations about repression during the Terror, the Law of 22 Prairial, and Thermidor.' Assign or allow students to choose partners and give each student a worksheet and pen.

Step 2 (10 minutes total gallery time): Start the timer. Students spend 1 minute at each station (6 stations). At each station pairs read the slip, write one short factual note that is grounded in the slip, and write one sentence that says whether the slip supports the idea that repression was widely supported by revolutionaries or shows disagreement among them. After 1 minute they rotate clockwise to the next station. While they move, quietly monitor timing and keep pairs on schedule with a 10-second warning before rotation.

Step 3 (1 minute debrief): When time is up, call students back to their seats. Ask two quick reporters (select one pair) to read one example of a slip that showed competing interpretations and one slip that gave a contested estimate of deaths. Collect worksheets or ask students to hold them up for later review.
activities.title: Gallery Walk: Comparing Claims about Repression, 1793–1794

differentiation.extension: Choose one station and write a 150-word paragraph comparing two interpretations of the same event mentioned on the slip (for example: was the Directory's property qualification designed to stabilise or to exclude?). Use at least one concrete piece of evidence from the slip and one other fact from your knowledge (map, army size, or date) to support each interpretation.
differentiation.support: If you are stuck, use this sentence frame for the alternative interpretation: 'This source shows ____, but a historian might argue instead that ____ because ____.' As a worked example: Station slip says 'revenge killings increased after Robespierre.' Write: Fact — 'There were revenge killings in southern France after Thermidor.' Interpretation — 'A historian might argue that these were local vendettas rather than centrally organised reprisals because local lists and court records show uneven timing.' Pair weaker readers with a stronger reader for each rotation.

materials: 6 printed evidence slips (one per station) — short excerpts or summaries
3 copies of a simple map of Revolutionary France (handout)
clipboards or hard surface for writing (one per pair)
timer or stopwatch (teacher's phone)
one worksheet per pair with four short questions and space for notes
student_instructions: Work with your partner. At each numbered station: 1) Read the short slip aloud. 2) On your worksheet answer: A) What factual claim does this slip make? (one sentence) B) What is one alternative interpretation or question a historian might raise about this claim? (one sentence). 3) If the slip names a place or army, mark it on your map and write a one-word label (e.g., 'army size', 'Thermidor revenge').

You have about two minutes at each station. When the teacher calls 'Move', go to the next numbered station. If you finish early, write one sentence suggesting why another historian might disagree with the slip.
Be prepared after the rotation to tell the class one surprising factual claim you found and one different interpretation you discussed.
success_criteria: Each pair has written a factual claim and an alternative interpretation for at least four different stations on their worksheet.
At least one pair can point to a station on their map and state the location mentioned (e.g., 'southern France', name on the slip).
During the quick whole-class share, at least two pairs offer a distinct alternative interpretation (not identical wording) to the slip's claim.
teacher_instructions: Before class: place the 6 evidence slips around the room (walls, desks). Each slip should be labeled Station 1–6 and contain a 2–4 sentence excerpt or summary tied to one concept: revenge killings in the south, a former Terror figure retaining office, Clause from Constitution Year III describing bicameral legislature, description of the five-director executive and property qualifications, a short report on mass mobilisation/army size and theatres, and a short passage about the 10 August 1792 insurrection and Louis XVI's fate. Give each pair a worksheet and a map copy.

Group students into pairs and say: 'You will move through six short evidence stations. At each station, read the slip, answer the two short questions on your worksheet, and mark on the map any place mentioned. You have 12 minutes total — two minutes per station plus time to move.' Start the timer and call 'Move' every two minutes.

While students rotate, circulate. At stations where confusion arises, read the slip aloud once and point students to which question on the worksheet asks for interpretation versus fact. If a pair finishes early at a station, ask them to identify one reason a historian might disagree with the source's claim.
When 12 minutes are up, call students back. Collect worksheets and quickly ask two pairs to share one piece of evidence that surprised them and one differing interpretation they noted.
activities.title: Thermidor Walk: Evidence Stations on Reaction, Constitution and War

differentiation.extension: Research and prepare a 90-second add-on (in the remaining class time) arguing how one symbol (guillotine or La Marseillaise) changed public reaction to policies like the abolition of slavery or the assignats; cite at least two passages from the slips and explain which interpretation of cause and effect you support and why.
differentiation.support: Pair a student who struggles to start with a stronger reader. Give this starter sentence frame: “My claim is ___. The passage says ‘___’ which shows ___. One other factor to consider is ___.” Provide one worked example: Pro claim — “Newspapers spread debate.” Passage quoted — “newspapers and pamphlets proliferated…stimulating revolutionary debate.” Explanation — “This shows print created a common forum for ideas.”

materials: One printed slip per student with a short quoted passage from the provided document (teacher prepares 10–12 different 1–2 sentence passages)
Stopwatch or classroom timer
Whiteboard or chart paper and marker
Paper and pens for students
student_instructions: 1. Read the passage on your slip. It is your evidence — you must reference it when you make a claim.

2. Your team argues either PRO (newspapers and pamphlets were the main driver of revolutionary change) or CON (other factors — symbols, women’s changing role, or economic policy — mattered as much or more).

3. Prepare up to three short points that each link a claim to a sentence from your slip. Write the sentence reference on your paper (e.g., “passage about assignats: ‘over-issuance caused hyperinflation’”).

4. When speaking: say your claim, read or summarise the passage you are using as evidence, then explain how that passage supports your claim. Example: “I claim newspapers spread debate. The passage says ‘newspapers and pamphlets proliferated…stimulating revolutionary debate,’ so newspapers helped spread ideas quickly.”
5. After the timed speeches, work with your team to write one sentence that uses at least one passage and also names one competing factor (symbols, women, or economy).
success_criteria: At least one student on each team quotes or paraphrases their passage aloud during a speech.
Each team produces a single sentence at the end that cites a passage and names a competing interpretation (for example: names the guillotine, La Marseillaise, assignats, or restrictions on women).
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students into two teams of equal size (debate Pro and Con) and hand each student a printed passage slip. Say: “You will use your passage as evidence in a short debate about whether newspapers and pamphlets were the main driver of revolutionary change compared with symbols, women’s activism, and economic policy.”

2. Give teams 4 minutes to read their slips, pick two speakers (one primary, one rebuttal), and prepare up to three evidence-backed points. Circulate, listening for claims tied to passages and prompting students to name the passage when they use it (for example: “The passage that says…”).

3. Run the debate: 2 minutes for the Pro team primary speaker, 1 minute for Con primary speaker, 2 minutes for Pro rebuttal, 1 minute for Con rebuttal. Use the timer and signal when each speaker starts and when 30 seconds remain.

4. After the debate, ask both teams to spend 2 minutes writing a single, shared sentence that uses at least one passage as evidence and acknowledges an alternative interpretation (for example: “Newspapers pushed debate, but symbols like the guillotine shaped popular perception”). Collect these sentences.

5. Close by reading two or three student sentences aloud and writing on the board one clear example named during the debate of how newspapers or pamphlets influenced public debate (teacher writes the specific example mentioned by students).
activities.title: Newspapers, Symbols, and Rights: A 12-Minute Class Debate

differentiation.extension: Compare two excerpts from different slips (ask a neighboring group to swap one excerpt). Decide which excerpt offers stronger evidence that the press caused long-term political change. Use the Acemoglu et al. citation as a prompt: what kind of data or long-term consequence would you look for to test the claim that pamphlets helped cause broad institutional change? Write a two-sentence plan describing one piece of evidence you would seek (e.g., circulation numbers, letters to officials, changes in legislation following a pamphlet campaign).
differentiation.support: If you are unsure how to start, use this sentence frame to pick a quote and decide: 'This sentence shows that newspapers/pamphlets ______ (gave people information / spread opinions / pressured leaders) because ______.' Example: 'This sentence shows that newspapers spread opinions because it says “the pamphlets argued that…”' Pair a struggling student with a stronger reader and assign roles: reader (reads excerpts), recorder (writes the quote), reporter (presents).

materials: One printed slip per group with three short excerpts from the document (see teacher instructions to prepare)
Timer or stopwatch (phone is fine)
One sheet of chart paper or a blank page per group
One pen or marker per group
student_instructions: In your group, read the three short excerpts on your slip aloud. Take turns so each person hears them.
Choose one short quoted sentence or phrase from the excerpts that most clearly shows how pamphlets or newspapers influenced public debate. Write that exact quote on your chart paper.

Decide together: does this excerpt suggest the press caused political change, reflected changes already happening, or both? Write one short sentence on the chart paper stating your choice and one reason from the quote.
Also write the name of one scholarly source that appears in your excerpts (for example: Chisick, Britannica, Opie, Acemoglu et al.).
Prepare to have one person present these three things in one minute: the quote, your chosen interpretation (caused / reflected / both) and the named source.
success_criteria: Each group has a chart paper with one exact quoted phrase from the excerpts visible.
Each group verbally states one clear interpretation (caused, reflected, or both) and gives a short reason tied to the quote during their one-minute report.
Each group identifies at least one named scholarly source from the excerpt (for example Chisick, Britannica, Opie, or Acemoglu et al.) on their paper or when speaking.
teacher_instructions: Before class (can be done in 10 minutes): cut the provided document into three short excerpts (each excerpt 2–3 short paragraphs). Choose excerpts that mention pamphlets/newspapers (Chisick), a specific example or named pamphlet or newspaper (from the compiled bibliography or Britannica passage), and a sentence that links press activity to consequences or public debate (for example a line that could be tied to Acemoglu et al. or Opie). Put the three excerpts together on one slip for each group.

Arrange students in groups of 3. Give each group one slip with the three excerpts, one sheet of chart paper, and one marker. Say: 'You have 10 minutes to read the excerpts, pick one direct sentence or phrase that shows how pamphlets or newspapers influenced public debate, and write that quote on your chart paper. Then write one short sentence that explains whether the excerpt shows the press caused change, reflected change, or both. Finally, note one scholarly source named in the excerpt.' Start the timer for 8 minutes (2 minutes for reporting).

While groups work, circulate. For each group, quietly confirm they have identified a specific quoted phrase from the excerpt, have written which named source is referenced (for example Chisick, Britannica, Opie, or Acemoglu et al.), and are deciding between the three causal interpretations (caused, reflected, both). If a group is stalled, read aloud one sentence from their slip and ask them which of the three interpretations it best supports.

When 8 minutes are up, call time. Ask three groups to each present in one minute: read their quoted phrase, state which interpretation they chose (caused / reflected / both) and name the scholarly source in the excerpt. Keep presentations to one minute each and use the last minute to thank groups and summarize that historians use the press as evidence but disagree on causation.
activities.title: Find the Evidence: How Pamphlets Shaped Debate

items.answer:
1) Population growth (social, long-term). Evidence: the document lists “population growth.” Analysis: rising population increased pressure on land and food supplies and raised demand for goods, intensifying social strain and competition for resources.

2) Economic recession and bad harvests (economic, short- to medium-term). Evidence: the document names “economic recession” and “bad harvests.” Analysis: poor harvests reduced grain supply and pushed up bread prices, while recession lowered incomes, together causing urban and rural hardship that fuelled unrest.

3) Tax complexity and unequal taxation (financial/economic, long-term). Evidence: the document refers to “tax complexity” and the tax system. Analysis: a cumbersome, unfair tax system left the privileged exempt or lightly taxed and placed heavy burdens on peasants and the bourgeoisie, creating widespread resentment.

4) Financial crisis/state debt (financial, short-term). Evidence: the document cites “financial” problems and resistance to fiscal reform. Analysis: large royal debt and repeated fiscal crises made government unable to govern effectively and forced attempts at reform that met opposition, triggering political crisis.

5) Resistance to reform by elites (political, short- to medium-term). Evidence: the document mentions “resistance to reform.” Analysis: when ministers or the king tried to introduce necessary fiscal and administrative reforms, privileged groups (e.g., parlements, nobility) blocked them, undermining the monarchy’s legitimacy and provoking confrontation.

6) Enlightenment ideas (political/social, long-term). Evidence: the document lists “Enlightenment ideas.” Analysis: spread of ideas about rights, representation and criticism of absolute monarchy changed public opinion, provided ideological tools for critics, and helped convert social and economic grievances into demands for political change.

rubric.criteria: Extent and quality of analysis: identification of multiple long-term and short-term social, economic, financial and political causes supported by specific evidence from the document and brief explanation of causal effect.

levels.descriptor: Identifies at least six distinct causes that cover social, economic, financial and political categories and both long- and short-term factors; for each factor quotes or names the specific evidence from the document and gives a clear, concise sentence explaining how that factor contributed to the Revolution.
levels.label: Excellent

levels.descriptor: Identifies 3–4 relevant causes with some coverage across the required categories; cites specific evidence from the document for most listed factors and gives brief but sometimes incomplete explanations of how they contributed.
levels.label: Partial

levels.descriptor: Identifies one or two vague or unsupported causes, fails to cite specific evidence from the document, or gives explanations that do not connect the factor to how it caused the Revolution.
levels.label: Minimal or Incorrect

items.stem: Using the document, analyse and list the multiple long-term and short-term social, economic, financial and political factors it identifies as causes of the French Revolution. For each factor you name, cite the specific evidence from the document and give a brief sentence explaining how that factor contributed. (6 marks)

items.answer: The Estates General was convened on 5 May 1789. Over the following weeks the Third Estate, frustrated by disputes over voting and representation in the Estates General, broke with the other orders. In June 1789 the Third Estate reconstituted itself as the National Assembly (commonly dated to mid‑June 1789), asserting that it represented the nation and claiming the right to make laws. Thus the calling of the Estates General on 5 May led, through the political conflict of May–June, to the Third Estate declaring itself the National Assembly in June 1789.

rubric.criteria: Shows the chronological link between the 5 May 1789 Estates General and the Third Estate's June 1789 declaration of the National Assembly, using dated actions and a causal explanation.

levels.descriptor: Clearly states that the Estates General opened on 5 May 1789 and explains that, after disputes over voting/representation, the Third Estate broke away and reconstituted itself as the National Assembly in June 1789; gives both dated actions and a causal link between them.
levels.label: Full credit

levels.descriptor: Mentions one correct dateed action (either 5 May 1789 or June 1789) and either describes the break by the Third Estate or gives a basic causal statement, but misses either one of the key dates or the clear causal link.
levels.label: Partial credit

levels.descriptor: Fails to give the correct dated actions (5 May 1789 and June 1789) or gives an answer that is historically incorrect or irrelevant to the sequence asked for.
levels.label: No credit

items.stem: Explain the sequence of events by which the Estates General of 1789 led to the Third Estate declaring itself the National Assembly. In your answer, give the specific dated actions from the period that show this development.

items.answer: The Terror combined large-scale, state-led arrests and executions (about 300,000 arrests and roughly 16,600 judicial executions) with contested estimates and episodes of localised violence (for example drownings at Nantes); it ended when Robespierre lost support, was arrested, wounded after an attempted suicide, and executed on 28 July 1794. Reason: This restates the documented figures and events and recognises both centralised repression and contested interpretations about methods and totals, plus the political fall of Robespierre at Thermidor.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Incorrect: This choice reflects the common misconception that all revolutionaries uniformly supported mass repression and that the figures were undisputed. The document shows the Terror involved organised arrests and executions but also contested death tolls and internal political conflict.
options.text: The Terror was a centrally organised campaign uniformly supported by all revolutionary leaders, carrying out consistent mass executions that left little dispute about the numbers arrested or killed.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Correct: This option matches the documented evidence: around 300,000 arrests and about 16,600 executions, acknowledged episodes of locally violent methods such as the drownings at Nantes and contested estimates, and the fall of Robespierre—arrest, injury after an attempted suicide, and execution on 28 July 1794.

items.answer: Between 1789 and July 1790 the Assembly took several decisive measures against the Catholic Church. First, it confiscated church property: national lands belonging to the Church were seized and declared biens nationaux to be sold to raise revenue for the state. Second, it abolished tithes, ending the compulsory money or produce payments that peasants had paid to support the clergy. Third, on 12 July 1790 the Assembly passed the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, which made clergy employees of the state: priests and bishops were to be elected, paid by the government, and required to swear an oath of loyalty to the nation. These actions were part of a broader programme (reflected in the August Decrees) that also abolished feudal privileges, asserted equality before the law, and opened public offices to all citizens. The document attributes a clear social consequence to these measures: they produced division and resistance among clergy and many Catholics. Making priests state officials and eliminating tithes undermined the traditional independence and authority of the Church and forced many clergy either to accept the new order or to refuse the oath. This split created a large group of “refractory” priests and alienated devout peasants and urban Catholics, contributing to social unrest, local protests, and in some regions to counter-revolutionary activity. In short, while the measures aimed at secularising Church wealth and bringing religion under state control, the immediate social consequence documented was a deepening of social and political divisions centred on faith and loyalty.

items.answer: The Storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789 became a lasting symbol of the French Revolution because the Bastille embodied royal authority, arbitrary power and the injustices of the Ancien Régime. Parisians attacked it to seize arms and gunpowder and to protest rising food prices and fears of a royal crackdown. Although the Bastille was popularly remembered as a large political prison, in reality it held very few prisoners at the time (only a handful, often reported as seven or fewer), so its importance was mainly symbolic rather than the liberation of many detainees. In the weeks after the attack the fortress was dismantled and its stones were distributed or displayed, reinforcing its role as a destroyed symbol of tyranny; the event also encouraged further revolutionary actions and helped spread unrest across France. Some historians stress its symbolic value and the power of public ritual, while others emphasise the practical motives (securing weapons) and the event’s role in accelerating local insurrections and political change.

items.answer: The Law of 22 Prairial drastically reduced legal protections for the accused and so made trials much faster and far more deadly. Specifically, it removed the right of defendants to call witnesses or have counsel, limited the possible verdicts essentially to "acquittal" or "guilty" with no nuanced judgments, and allowed the Revolutionary Tribunal to convict on moral evidence or general suspicion rather than detailed proof. Procedural safeguards such as examination of evidence and the hearing of defence arguments were curtailed, and trials were shortened so that verdicts and executions followed quickly. Contextually, this law was passed when the Committee of Public Safety sought to speed up the processing of suspected "enemies of the people": historians note that after the law was enacted the number of people sent from Paris to the guillotine rose sharply, because the Tribunal could try many more cases in a short time and convict on vague charges. Some historians interpret the law as a deliberate move by revolutionary leaders to concentrate power and remove obstacles to mass repression; others argue it was an emergency response to perceived internal threats. Either way, by removing defence rights and simplifying verdicts the law materially accelerated executions in Paris.

items.answer: After Robespierre’s fall the Thermidorian Reaction produced contrasting outcomes. Regionally, there were violent reprisals against Jacobins: in parts of southern France revenge killings and local uprisings targeted known supporters of the Terror, producing a wave of partisan violence. Politically, however, national control shifted without a complete purge of all Revolutionary officials: many former Terror figures managed to keep or regain positions as the Convention and committees reasserted moderate control, and power moved toward more conservative and property‑owning groups rather than a full return to pre‑Revolution institutions. Thus the aftermath combined local vengeance and violence with a political reorientation and selective survival of some former Terror actors.

items.answer: The Revolutionary Wars transformed French warfare by mobilising large citizen armies and by spreading conflict across Europe and beyond, which in turn enabled France to annex territory and set up satellite states. Mobilisation: after 1792 the French government raised huge forces through measures such as the levée en masse (1793) and broader conscription policies, producing armies far larger than the professional forces of earlier wars. These mass armies provided the manpower to sustain long campaigns and replace losses, changing the scale of operations. Multiple theatres: France fought on many fronts — northern Europe and the Low Countries, the Rhine frontier and German states, Italy (notably Napoleon’s campaigns 1796–97), Spain and Portugal, and even overseas expeditions such as Egypt (1798). Examples of annexation and satellites: in 1795 the Dutch Republic was replaced by the Batavian Republic under French influence; in Italy Napoleon’s victories led to the creation of the Cisalpine Republic (1797) and other sister republics; the French also annexed territories on the left bank of the Rhine and made territorial gains after treaties such as Campo Formio (1797). Causation: the large conscript armies made it possible to fight simultaneously in multiple theatres and to garrison occupied regions, enabling France to impose political changes and administrative control. Interpretations differ: some historians stress ideological aims (spreading revolutionary institutions), while others emphasise strategic and economic motives (securing buffers and resources). Both factors operated together: military capacity created by mobilisation gave France the means to export revolution or to secure its borders through annexation and client states.

After 1789 the Revolutionary government nationalised church lands and later properties of émigrés to secure state finances. To mobilise this wealth quickly it issued assignats — paper notes initially presented as certificates backed by confiscated land. Contemporary records show the assignats were intended both as government bonds and as currency to pay debts and military expenses. One interpretation is that assignats were a pragmatic short-term solution: they increased liquidity, allowed the government to meet obligations, and transferred property into the hands of new owners, supporting revolutionary goals.

However, from 1790–1796 the government issued ever larger quantities of assignats to cover chronic budget deficits. Historians point to over-issuance as the central cause of their collapse: as the supply of notes swelled beyond the value of available land, confidence fell, prices rose, and hyperinflation followed. Evidence for this includes rapidly rising price indices and contemporary complaints about falling real wages and market instability. Another interpretation emphasises structural pressures — war expenditure, tax collection failure, and political instability — arguing these forced excessive issuance and made any paper currency unreliable. Both views are compatible: over-issuance was the proximate cause, while fiscal and political weaknesses were underlying drivers.

The collapse had major economic and social effects. Economically it produced rampant inflation, disrupted commerce, and wiped out savings for many urban and rural households. Socially it fuelled hardship among the poor and anger among the middle classes who lost property value, contributing to unrest and undermining the Revolution's legitimacy in some areas. In sum, assignats began as a land-backed financing measure but, through over-issuance amid fiscal and political crisis, became a cause of severe economic dislocation with important social and political consequences.

items.answer: Chisick shows that royalist pamphlets and periodicals such as the Ami du Roi, produced from Abbé Royou’s offices, aimed to shape public opinion by mobilising readers through targeted messaging and by creating a networked distribution of print. First, they used clear, persuasive argument and moralising rhetoric to defend monarchy and religion, presenting the king as a guarantor of order and criticising revolutionary excesses. Second, they deployed selective reporting and satire: regular periodical formats (weekly essays, letters, and polemical pamphlets) repeated themes, attacked leading revolutionary figures, and used caricature and anecdote to make complex arguments accessible to literate urban readers. Chisick also emphasises the organisational tactics — centralised printing, paid contributors, and connections with provincial booksellers — which broadened reach beyond Paris. However, these royalist efforts faced important limitations: they competed in an expanding, crowded print market dominated increasingly by revolutionary voices; their social base was narrower (more aristocratic, clerical, and moderate bourgeois readers), and censorship or association with counter-revolution made distribution risky. Thus while royalist journalism tried to influence opinion through rhetorical clarity, regular publication, and distribution networks, its effectiveness was constrained by competition, limited audience, and political danger.

Two major historiographical themes in the bibliography are: 1) social and class-based interpretations of the Revolution, and 2) cultural, political culture, and intellectual approaches.

1) Social and class-based interpretations — exemplar: Albert Soboul, The French Revolution, 1787–1799 (or Soboul’s work on the Sans-culottes and social classes). Soboul’s work focuses on class structures, popular movements, and the role of the urban working classes (the sans-culottes) in driving the Revolution. This fits the social-history theme because it explains events in terms of socio-economic interests, class conflict, and collective action rather than solely elite politics. The bibliography’s inclusion of Soboul indicates attention to Marxist-influenced and social causation explanations.

2) Cultural, political culture, and intellectual approaches — exemplar: Lynn Hunt, Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (or Hunt’s writings on political culture and the public sphere). Hunt emphasizes language, symbols, public rituals, and changing mentalities, using cultural sources (pamphlets, festivals, petitions) to show how political meanings were constructed. This fits the cultural/intellectual theme by treating ideology, discourse, and practices as causal factors in revolutionary change rather than only structural social forces. Its presence in the bibliography signals interest in cultural analysis and interdisciplinary methods (literary, anthropological approaches) in interpreting the Revolution.

Together these examples show that the bibliography covers competing interpretations — structural class-based analyses and cultural/ideational approaches — and hence provides students with contrasting frameworks for understanding causes and dynamics of the French Revolution.

1. Population growth — evidence: the document names "population growth." Analysis: a long-term social and economic pressure that increased demand for food and strained resources, contributing to unrest. (1 mark)

4. Tax complexity (and likely unfair taxation) — evidence: the document mentions "tax complexity." Analysis: a long-term financial and political problem that made revenue collection inefficient, increased burdens on the Third Estate, and fuelled resentment toward the fiscal system. (1 mark)

5. Resistance to reform — evidence: the document states "resistance to reform." Analysis: a political and institutional cause (long-term) showing that attempts to change taxation and governance were blocked by vested interests (nobility, clergy), producing constitutional crisis. (1 mark)

6. Enlightenment ideas — evidence: the document includes "Enlightenment ideas." Analysis: a long-term intellectual and political factor that changed political expectations about rights, sovereignty and legitimacy and helped justify revolutionary action. (1 mark)

Overall, the document identifies a mix of long-term structural causes (population growth, tax complexity, resistance to reform, Enlightenment ideas) and shorter-term economic shocks (recession, bad harvests) that together explain why revolution became possible and then immediate.

items.answer: On 5 May 1789 the Estates General met at Versailles, summoned because of the fiscal crisis. Early debates revealed a dispute over voting procedures: the First and Second Estates wanted voting by order while the Third Estate demanded voting by head so it could have greater influence. Because the Estates General failed to resolve this dispute, the Third Estate moved to act independently. On 17 June 1789 the deputies of the Third Estate declared themselves the National Assembly, claiming they represented the nation and had the authority to make laws. Their declaration was a direct response to the stalemate over voting and the refusal of the privileged orders to accept common deliberation. When the King and some privileged deputies tried to prevent this break, the National Assembly found its meeting rooms closed and on 20 June 1789 the deputies assembled in a nearby indoor tennis court and took the Tennis Court Oath, vowing not to separate until they had given France a constitution. Thus the sequence is: 5 May 1789 (Estates General convened and voting dispute became clear) → continued deadlock → 17 June 1789 (Third Estate proclaims the National Assembly) → 20 June 1789 (Tennis Court Oath, which consolidated the break and commitment to constitutional reform).

The Reign of Terror was large in both scale and intensity. Between September 1793 and July 1794 around 300,000 people were arrested and about 16,600 officially executed for counter‑revolutionary activity, showing systematic use of state arrest and capital punishment. Repressive mechanisms included legal instruments (revolutionary tribunals), mass arrests, and extra-judicial or semi-official violence such as the drownings at Nantes; the latter illustrate that repression took both formal and brutal local forms and that some death toll estimates remain contested by historians. 

There are two main competing interpretations. One sees the Terror as driven by a revolutionary leadership convinced of existential threats: war, royalist plots and aristocratic resistance justified harsh centralised measures to defend the Republic. This interpretation emphasises central institutions (committees, tribunals) and the stated aim of protecting the revolution. The alternative interpretation stresses factional politics and power struggles within the revolution: the Terror became a tool for political actors to eliminate rivals, with local initiatives and rivalries contributing to violence. Evidence for this includes the contested death estimates and episodes of localized excess (e.g., Nantes) that suggest not all repression was centrally directed or universally supported. 

Thermidor shows the political contingency: Robespierre lost support, was arrested after political isolation, wounded in an attempted suicide at the Hôtel de Ville, and executed on 28 July 1794 with colleagues. His fall supports the view that the Terror involved intense internal conflict, not unanimous revolutionary agreement. In sum, the Terror combined centralised institutions and legal repression with local violence and factional motives; historians should therefore combine both interpretations rather than treat the Terror as either purely defensive state policy or only elite power‑struggles.

Evaluates two competing interpretations (defensive revolutionary policy vs. factional power struggles), cites evidence for each, and explains how Thermidor and Robespierre's arrest/execution support the conclusion that both central policy and internal conflict were important.

Analysis is present but lacks depth or specific evidence.

teacher_script.board_action: Write: "Quick recap: Storming of the Bastille; Estates General called (May 1789)."
teacher_script.heading: Recap and share one prior fact
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We are continuing from Origins and Opening Acts. In one sentence please read your entry ticket aloud when I point to you. After three people, I will ask for one factual correction or addition." Point to student A, B, C to read. After three, say: "Quick class check: who can state one clear fact about the Storming of the Bastille or the role of the Estates General?" Accept one-sentence answers. If a student says 'the Estates General voted as one body', correct: "Remember: it met in three estates and how they voted was the dispute — we will return to that."

anticipated_questions: Why did the Third Estate declare itself the National Assembly?
Did the National Assembly cause the Bastille to be stormed?
Are the arrest and execution numbers exact?
teacher_script.board_action: Write dated sequence as bullets and the Reign of Terror definition and numbers.
teacher_script.heading: Teacher presentation: Estates General → National Assembly and dates
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Listen as I tell a short sequence of dated steps. I will point at the dates on the board. Follow along and underline any word you don't know." Read clearly: "May 1789: King summons the Estates General, a body that last met in 1614 and which had three estates — clergy, nobility, Third Estate. Voting procedures were contested: the Third Estate wanted to vote by head, not by estate. In June 1789 the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly, saying it represented the nation and would act as a constituent authority. Urban unrest followed, including the Storming of the Bastille in July, and the Assembly then moved to radical changes including the August Decrees." Then say: "Now a short factual overview of the Reign of Terror: from September 1793 to July 1794 revolutionary authorities arrested about 300,000 people and executed roughly 16,600 for counter-revolutionary activity. These are the numbers historians use as evidence; there are also different interpretations about why the Terror happened." Pause and ask: "Which date marks the start of the Terror? Which body declared itself in June 1789?"

anticipated_questions: How do we decide long-term vs short-term?
Can one cause be both long-term and short-term?
What counts as a good quote for evidence?
teacher_script.board_action: Write group labels: A: population growth, B: bad harvests, C: tax system, D: Enlightenment. Under each, leave space for students to add one quoted evidence line.
teacher_script.heading: Small-group source analysis: causes (long-term vs short-term)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Form groups of four. Each group gets one short extract to read: population growth; bad harvests and economic recession; tax system and resistance to reform; Enlightenment ideas. Read the extract aloud once (2 minutes). Then mark whether the extract describes a long-term cause or a short-term trigger and copy one line of evidence from the extract that supports your choice (6 minutes). I will circulate and listen to one group's reasoning. Be ready to report: your cause, long-term or short-term, and one quoted line as evidence (4 minutes)." Walk to groups, listen, and prompt with: "Which phrase shows time length? Where in the text does it say immediate impact?"

anticipated_questions: Can we use different evidence than our small-group extract?
Who were the moderates and who were the radicals?
Does debating mean we choose a side as our real belief?
teacher_script.board_action: Write debate roles and timing: "Moderates: statement 2', evidence 2', rebuttal 1' — Radicals: same."
teacher_script.heading: Structured role-play debate: moderates vs radicals
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Now split the class into two halves: moderates and radicals. Moderates argue that the National Assembly's steps were careful and did not justify extraordinary emergency measures. Radicals argue that the political crisis and threats made emergency measures likely. Use your group's evidence from the extracts: each side gets two minutes to state their main point and one piece of quoted evidence. Then each side gets one minute to rebut. Follow this script: statement (2 min), evidence read (2 min), rebuttal (1 min). I will time and call for the rebuttal. Begin." Circulate, remind students to name the cause they cite and to quote the line they used in the small-group activity. If students fall into the misconception that the Terror had united support, ask: "Where in our evidence do we see disagreements among revolutionaries?"

anticipated_questions: How long do the answers need to be?
Do I have to write dates for both answers?
What if I can't remember an exact phrase for evidence?
teacher_script.board_action: Write exit task instructions exactly as students must copy them.
teacher_script.heading: Check for understanding: exit questions
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "On a slip of paper, write three short answers: (1) List two causes of the Revolution and one short piece of evidence for each (one phrase each). (2) Write one dated step showing how the Estates General became the National Assembly (one line)." Collect slips or have students drop them in the tray. If a student writes only 'the Terror was supported by all revolutionaries,' ask them to add a line noting a division (for example, factions or Robespierre vs Hébertists)."

anticipated_questions: How long should the paragraph be?
Can we use class notes or must we quote the extract?
What if we disagree with the interpretations?
teacher_script.board_action: Write homework: "One-paragraph: pick one cause, cite one quote from today's extracts, explain link to later events. Due next class."
teacher_script.heading: Consolidate and assign homework
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We covered the sequence from the Estates General to the National Assembly and the Reign of Terror's scope. Two interpretations stand out: (1) the Terror resulted from coherent central policy, and (2) it resulted from internal divisions, emergency pressures and contested decisions. For homework, write one paragraph citing one cause from today and explain, with one quoted line of evidence from today's extracts, how that cause helped lead to later events. That will prepare you for the Declaration of the Rights of Man next lesson." Repeat the homework exactly and tell students where to hand it in.

bullet_points: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen — issued by the National Assembly.
August Decrees: Legislation published by the Assembly that abolished feudalism and cancelled church tithes, and enacted equality before the law and other measures.

Civil Constitution of the Clergy (12 July 1790): Assembly confiscated church property, abolished tithes, and made clergy employees of the state; produced division and resistance among clergy and Catholics.
Example sequence: Estates-General → National Assembly → urban unrest (Bastille) → August Decrees.
Group questions: 1) What effects do the sources claim? 2) What voices or consequences are missing?
Class summary: Documents claim legal equality and state revenue; missing/competing views include loss of local religious authority, refusal of oath by many priests, and uneven benefits for peasants.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: They confiscated church property, cancelled/abolished tithes, and passed the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (which made clergy employees of the state). Any two of these are correct.
checkpoint_questions.question: Name two concrete measures the Assembly took against the Catholic Church described in this period.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: The class sources say these measures caused division and resistance among clergy and Catholics, unrest in parishes, and loss of trust in the Revolution — for example, priests refusing to accept state pay and peasants resisting reforms.
checkpoint_questions.question: According to the sources used in class, what is one social consequence the Assembly or its critics claimed followed from confiscating church property and abolishing tithes?

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: The excerpt downplays local peasant views and the practical impact of lost church charity; it may present the reform as orderly while ignoring violent resistance, émigré clergy, or how poorer people relied on the Church’s services.
checkpoint_questions.question: Give one silence or bias you can detect in the Civil Constitution excerpt we read (what the source does not show or downplays).

entry_ticket.expected_response: Common answer (misconception): "Peasants gain because they no longer pay tithes." A more accurate response: "The state and buyers of former church land gain money and power; many peasants may still lose local rights or face new rents or sell-offs; clergy lose status and income."
entry_ticket.prompt: If the National Assembly (1) cancels church tithes and (2) seizes church land to sell, who do you think immediately gains and who loses? Circle one: peasants / clergy / nobles / state. Then write one short reason for your choice (one sentence).

exit_ticket.prompt: Write one clear social consequence the class sources attribute to the Assembly’s church reforms (confiscation of property, abolition of tithes, Civil Constitution of the Clergy). Then give one alternative interpretation or a perspective the sources leave out.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Response names a social consequence linked to the reforms (for example: increased division/resistance among clergy and Catholics, parish unrest, loss of church charity) and then adds a plausible alternative or missing perspective (for example: peasants may have welcomed land redistribution; sources ignore women’s experience; the state’s administrative view).

homework.submission_format: Typed or handwritten paragraph plus citation; bring the quotation printed or written down.
tasks: Write a one-page (250–300 words) paragraph that: a) lists the three measures against the Church from class, b) explains one social consequence the sources attribute to those measures, and c) notes one perspective missing from those sources and why it matters.

Bring to class one short primary-source quotation (1–2 sentences) about the Church from a textbook or an online archive (cite the source). Be ready to say whether it supports or challenges the class sources.

mentor_moment.story: A history teacher once asked students whose grandparents had kept old family prayers. Several said those practices continued even when laws changed; people kept the ritual if it met daily needs.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Legal change can be swift, but social habits and local needs often determine how people actually respond.

anticipated_questions: Student: "Which estate were parish priests in?" Anticipated: "Some parish priests were from the Third Estate; higher clergy were Second Estate."
Student: "Was the Bastille part of the Estates-General?" Anticipated: "No — the Bastille was an event of urban unrest that influenced the Assembly."
Student: "Do tithes apply to everyone?" Anticipated: "Tithes were payments to the Church that affected many peasants, but how they were enforced varied by region."
teacher_script.board_action: Write three one-line prompts for students to copy. Underline today: 'What the Assembly did to the Church; social consequences.'
teacher_script.heading: Activate prior knowledge and quick recap
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Take out your entry ticket answers. I will call three people to read one short line each: say who you circled and one reason. (Choose 3 volunteers.)" After each volunteer: "Quick check — which estate did clergy belong to? (Point at students: 'First, Second, or Third estate?')" Then ask three quick prompts aloud, waiting for thumbs-up/ thumbs-down: 1) "The Estates-General met because of a financial crisis — true or false?" 2) "The Third Estate claimed political representation — true or false?" 3) "Urban unrest (for example the storming of the Bastille) pushed the Assembly to act — true or false?" If a student answers false, ask them to say why briefly. Close: "Today we'll look at what the Assembly actually did to the Church and how people reacted."

anticipated_questions: Student: "Did the Assembly take property right away?" Anticipated: "The text says the Assembly confiscated church property — that was a legal action that then led to sales and redistribution."
Student: "What does 'employees of the state' mean for priests?" Anticipated: "It means priests would be paid by the state and required to swear loyalty to the Constitution, which many resisted."
Student: "Are the August Decrees the same as the Declaration?" Anticipated: "No — the Declaration is a statement of rights; the August Decrees are specific laws abolishing feudalism and tithes."
teacher_script.board_action: Write the three short headings and one quoted phrase under each: Declaration; August Decrees (use the exact definition); Civil Constitution of the Clergy (write 12 July 1790 and 'clergy employees of the state').
teacher_script.heading: Teacher-led evidence session: read key primary excerpts
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "I will read three short excerpts. Listen for actions taken and any stated reasons. After each reading I will ask one question." Read aloud (slowly, clearly): 1) A line introducing the Declaration: "The National Assembly issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen." Pause and ask: "What right or idea in the phrase 'Rights of Man and of the Citizen' might challenge church privilege?" 2) A line identifying the August Decrees: "August Decrees: Legislation published by the Assembly that abolished feudalism and cancelled church tithes, and enacted equality before the law and other measures." Pause and ask: "Which two concrete measures do you hear in that sentence?" 3) A short line on the Civil Constitution of the Clergy: "The Assembly confiscated church property, abolished tithes, and enacted the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (12 July 1790) making clergy employees of the state; this produced division and resistance among clergy and Catholics." Pause and ask: "What is one immediate legal change described here?" After the three, summarize aloud: "So the documents name (a) Declaration, (b) August Decrees ending feudal rights and tithes, and (c) seizure of church property plus Civil Constitution making clergy state employees."

anticipated_questions: Student: "What counts as a 'claimed effect'?" Anticipated: "Anything the source says will happen or be solved, for example 'equality before the law' or 'state revenue increases.'"
Student: "How do we identify bias?" Anticipated: "Look for who benefits in the text, who is named or unnamed, and whether the text admits problems or not."
Student: "Can we say a missing perspective is peasants even if not mentioned?" Anticipated: "Yes — if the source focuses on legal change but not daily life, peasants could be a missing perspective."
teacher_script.board_action: Write two guiding questions: '1) What effects do the sources claim follow from these measures?' '2) What voices or consequences are missing or understated?'
teacher_script.heading: Group source analysis (small groups)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Form groups of 3-4. Give each group two short excerpts: one describing confiscation/abolition of tithes and one from the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Your task: (1) list two claimed effects these sources say will happen, and (2) name one thing the sources do not mention or might be biased about. Use the evidence in the excerpts to support your answers. I'll write two guiding questions on the board. You have 10 minutes to discuss and 2 minutes to write a quick public note to post on the wall." Walk among groups, prompt with: "Where does the document say the money goes? Who might oppose this change and why?" If a group gets stuck, read a sentence from the excerpt and ask them to underline the verbs.

anticipated_questions: Student (priest role): "Can we say all peasants resisted?" Anticipated: "You should say some peasants resisted while others accepted changes; use evidence or note silence."
Student (official role): "Did selling land help the national budget right away?" Anticipated: "The sources claim revenue, but students may question timing and distribution."
Student in audience: "Are priests allowed to refuse being state employees?" Anticipated: "Many priests refused to swear the oath; that refusal created division and resistance among Catholics."
teacher_script.board_action: Draw two columns titled 'Priests/Peasants' and 'Officials/Landowners' and quickly jot one evidence phrase each side cites during presentations.
teacher_script.heading: Role-play debate: social consequences and resistance
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Two larger groups will present: Group A = parish priests and Catholic peasants; Group B = revolutionary officials and landowners. Each side has 3 minutes total: 1 minute to state your main claim, 2 minutes to cite one piece of evidence from the excerpts and answer a quick question from me. Start with Group A." Call on the two spokespersons. After each short presentation ask one pointed question: to priests/peasants: "Which social consequence worried you most?" to officials/landowners: "How did you justify selling church land to gain revenue?" Remind both sides to use the excerpt evidence and to note where sources skip a viewpoint.

anticipated_questions: Student: "Can my alternative be about the economy?" Anticipated: "Yes — an economic or social missing perspective is valid if you explain why it's missing from the sources."

Student: "Will these disagreements cause the Terror?" Anticipated: "They help explain some causes of later repression, but the next lesson will show the direct links and specific laws like the Law of 22 Prairial."
Student: "Do we hand in the exit sentence?" Anticipated: "Yes, I will collect these as the individual exit ticket."
teacher_script.board_action: Under the two columns add a final line: 'Class sources: legal equality, revenue, end of tithes' and 'Missing/competing views: local unrest, religious division, uneven benefit.'
teacher_script.heading: Individual check + teacher consolidation and bridge
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Write one clear social consequence the class sources attribute to the church reforms (one sentence). Then write one alternative interpretation or a perspective the sources miss (one sentence)." Give 3 minutes writing time. After 3 minutes collect a few samples aloud: read 2 student answers (one that follows the sources and one that offers a missing perspective). Finish with a 1-minute summary: "Competing interpretations: Documents present legal changes and claim equality and revenue. Critics and many clergy saw loss of religious freedom and local stability. Those disagreements help explain later repression during the Terror and the Thermidor reaction."

Drownings at Nantes — primary account: mass executions by drowning (method highlighted)
Law of 22 Prairial (1794): denied accused 'enemies of the people' the right to defend themselves
Robespierre: arrested, taken to Hotel de Ville, injured after attempting suicide, executed 28 July

Group C claim — (example) 'Robespierre lost support' — Evidence: arrest narrative; factions vs him — Alternative: personal rivals used repression to remove him

Column comparison: left column 'Evidence' (drownings, law text, arrest account) vs right column 'Interpretations' (central policy vs local violence; legal change = acceleration vs emergency measure; fall = loss of support vs political purge).

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Evidence 1: Accounts of drownings at Nantes — these describe mass, local executions carried out by representatives and local officials, showing repression could be organised outside Paris. Evidence 2: Text or summary of the Law of 22 Prairial — this law removed defendants' rights to defend themselves in Paris trials, showing a central legal change that sped up executions. Each shows a different mechanism: local massacres and centralised legal acceleration.
checkpoint_questions.question: Using the primary-source extracts on drownings at Nantes and the Law of 22 Prairial, which pieces of evidence would you use to support a claim that the Terror involved both local violence and central legal changes? Give two pieces of evidence and explain briefly how each supports the claim.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Best fit: the documents show political divisions and inconsistent policy. Supporting detail: evidence of conflict between revolutionary factions (e.g., references to Hébertists vs moderates, or differing accounts of Robespierre's motives and actions) and the narrative of Robespierre losing support before Thermidor suggests internal disagreement rather than total unity. Alternatively, if a student chooses the unified-policy view, they must cite high execution statistics plus the Law of 22 Prairial as centralising force.
checkpoint_questions.question: One historian argues the high death toll estimates show a unified revolutionary policy of mass extermination; another argues the evidence shows political divisions and inconsistent policy. Which interpretation fits the documents you studied best, and what is one specific document detail that supports that interpretation?

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Explanation: Robespierre's arrest and execution show he had lost support among other revolutionaries, so Thermidor can be seen as a political reaction against his leadership and policies. Limitation: the episode alone doesn't prove broader public opinion or structural factors (war, economic strain, provincial resistance) caused Thermidor; it may reflect elite power struggles more than wider causes.
checkpoint_questions.question: Explain briefly how Robespierre's arrest and execution (as described in the extracts) can be used to explain a cause of Thermidor. State one limitation of using that episode alone to explain the end of the Terror.

entry_ticket.expected_response: A useful response names one of: a single leader (e.g. Robespierre), a committee or groups (e.g. Committee of Public Safety, local Revolutionary Tribunals), or many officials (local representatives, municipal authorities). The underlined certainty should reveal students' confidence (common wrong answer: 'definitely a single leader' which signals the misconception of unified control).
entry_ticket.prompt: Write one short sentence answering: "Who decided to execute people during the Terror — a single leader, a group, or many different officials?" Then underline the one word that shows how sure you are (e.g., definitely, probably, maybe).

exit_ticket.prompt: Write a short analytical paragraph (4–6 sentences) that answers: To what extent did the Law of 22 Prairial change how the Terror worked, and how does this compare with evidence of local violent practices like the drownings at Nantes? Use at least one specific detail from the documents.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Paragraph states a clear judgement about the Law of 22 Prairial's impact (e.g., it accelerated judicial executions by removing defence rights) and compares that central legal change to local practices (e.g., drownings at Nantes were extra-legal or locally organised). Includes at least one specific document detail (date/name of law; a phrase or fact about Nantes drownings) and a sentence noting a limitation or alternative interpretation (e.g., internal divisions or differing scales).

homework.submission_format: Written paragraphs (digital or handwritten scanned PDF).
tasks: Write a one-page (≈250–350 words) answer to: 'Which mattered more in increasing executions during the Terror — legal changes like the Law of 22 Prairial or local acts of violence? Use two pieces of evidence from the period's documents and explain an alternate interpretation.'

Select one primary-source extract from today's set and annotate it: underline two phrases that show perspective or bias, write one sentence on the author's possible motive, and one sentence on how that affects using the extract as evidence.

mentor_moment.story: A historian once showed a classroom two lists: one of laws passed in Paris and one of local letters reporting massacres. Students realised the laws looked neat but the letters showed messy fights and fear on the ground.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Laws tell you what leaders intended; local accounts show what actually happened. Use both to reach a balanced judgement.
